newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Africa Israel under fire over Sabbath.
newsitem.headline: Africa Israel under fire over Sabbath.

text.p: What price religion?

That's the question investors have been asking since a religious Jew bought a controlling stake in Africa Israel Investment Ltd three months ago and started to bring its policy in line with Orthodox beliefs, share analysts said on Wednesday.

Under Lev Leviev's stewardship, the Tel Aviv-traded property development firm decided a shopping mall planned for an upscale, secular neighbourhood of the city would be closed on the Jewish Sabbath, a move that grabbed headlines in Israel.

A battle for the soul of the Jewish state has been raging for decades. But in the case of Africa Israel, whose share price has dipped by as much as 25 percent since Leviev took over, the bottom line is whether religion is good for business.

"Revenues are hit if you don't work on Saturdays. Investors believe the company's business will be hurt and that is why the share price has dropped," Danny Zacharia of Capital Holdings said on Wednesday.
Doron Tsur, head of research at Sahar Securities, said investors were concerned "that management is working along ideological rather than business lines".
He said media reports that some top managers were quitting, apparently over the Sabbath policy, were also depressing the share price on the Tel Aviv stock exchange.

Ritual Jewish law bans work on the Sabbath running from Friday evening to Saturday night. But most Israelis are not religious and many flock to the several shopping centres that have opened their doors on Saturdays.
Africa Israel, whose business empire includes hotels and petrol stations, came under more public pressure on Wednesday.

Legislator Shalom Simchon of the main opposition Labour party said he had asked the Securities Authority to examine whether Leviev and the company's directors made "proper disclosure" about his Sabbath policies when he bought the firm.

"If this was his intention when he purchased the company from Bank Leumi, which is owned by the state, I think he needed to disclose this under law," Simchon told Reuters. "The steps he has taken are hurting the small investor."
Simchon said authorities should consider stopping trading in Africa Israel on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange "to determine if its directors are acting in the interests of shareholders".
The Authority does not comment on its investigations.
Israeli newspapers, meanwhile, are fuelling the controversy and investor jitters with reports that the company will no longer keep sales offices at its residential building sites open on Saturdays.
The newspapers also said Africa Israel had unsuccessfully pressured its partner in a chain of petrol stations to close them on the Sabbath.
Africa Israel officials did not return repeated calls for comment. The company's share was up 2.75 percent, at 21,577 agorot, in late trading on the Tel Aviv exchange on Wednesday.

Last week, Africa Israel managing director Avigdor Kaplan, appointed on January 29, the same day Leviev was named company chairman, shrugged off the criticism saying the company was guided by professional considerations.

Leviev, who was a leading figure in the Israeli diamond industry, paid $141 million for a stake of Africa Israel from Leumi and another $49 million for shares controlled by Israeli businessmen Mordechai Zisser and Eitan Wertheimer.
The combined stakes were equal to 46.58 percent of equity in Africa and 54.2 percent of voting rights.
Leumi, which previously controlled Africa Israel, was forced to reduce its stake to 25 percent under bank reform laws and will have to reduce it to 20 percent by 1999.
